codex: Spring's first vegetable. The shoot is a promise the whole grove keeps — peel it, boil it, and it feeds you like grain.
description: a pale pointed shoot pushing up through leaf litter

knowledgeLevels.1: Bamboo shoot. Pale, pointed, pushing out of the ground near the poles.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the tender shoot (peel the sheaths, eat the core). Raw shoots carry taxiphyllin — a cyanide compound. Boiling destroys it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: boil 20-30 minutes and discard the water. Slice thin for soup, chunk for stew. A spring staple — harvest daily while they come.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: take shoots under 30cm, snap-clean at the base. Boil with the lid off. 2x yield from a good brake.

lookalikeNote: Only take shoots you watched emerge from a food bamboo. Ornamental bamboos run far more bitter and toxic — if you didn't see it planted as food, leave it.
name: Bamboo Shoot
preparation: Peel the tough sheaths, slice, and boil 20-30 minutes; discard the water. Never eat raw.
sources: National Geographic — bamboo shoots superfood piece

uses.note: boiled shoots; soup and stew vegetable

codex: The paddies went wild years ago. The rice didn't get the memo — it still heads, still fills, still feeds whoever bothers to thresh it.
description: a grass with drooping seed heads standing in shallow water

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild rice. A grass standing in the shallows with heavy seed heads.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the grain (thresh and winnow the heads). Needs cooking — boil like any rice.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: real calories, stores for months dry. Harvest when the heads droop and grains fall at a touch.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: beat the heads into a basket at dawn (dew keeps them from shattering early). Parboil before hulling. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Feral rice shatters — the grains fall at a touch when ripe. If the heads hold their grain tight, it's a planted variety gone weedy, still edible.
name: Feral Rice
preparation: Strip the heads, thresh, winnow, boil. The hulls are silica-sharp — winnow well.

uses.note: boiled grain; the region's staple starch

codex: The terraces went to seed but the bushes never stopped flushing. Two leaves and a bud — the old picking rhyme still works.
description: a waist-high bush with glossy oval leaves on terraced ground

knowledgeLevels.1: Tea bush. Glossy oval leaves, terraces gone wild.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the young flush — two leaves and a bud. Steep, don't gorge: caffeine and tannins.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: brewed tea for alertness and morale; chewed leaves for the trail. Wilt then heat the leaves to keep it green.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick at dawn in spring for the sweetest flush. Dry for storage. A rested mind forages better.

lookalikeNote: True tea has glossy evergreen leaves with finely serrated edges and a pale underside. If the leaf crushes without that clean tea smell, it's an imposter.
name: Tea Bush
preparation: Steep the young leaves; chew sparingly. Caffeine and tannins — a handful brewed is medicine, a basket eaten is a mistake.

uses.note: brewed; chewed sparingly on the trail

codex: Fall's candy, and it hangs on the tree into winter — nature's own pantry. The astringent ones teach patience; the ripe ones teach gratitude.
description: a tree hung with orange globes among broad dark leaves

knowledgeLevels.1: Persimmon. Orange fruit, still hard on the tree.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the fruit — eat only when soft and wrinkled. Unripe = a mouthful of chalk (tannins).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: high sugar, vitamin A and C. Hangs on the tree into winter — harvest through the cold months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: frost sweetens them. Dry halved ripe fruit for winter stores. 2x yield from the old orchard trees.

lookalikeNote: Wait for the fruit to go soft and wrinkled — or for frost. An unripe persimmon's tannins will turn your mouth inside out. Ripe ones are honey.
name: Asian Persimmon
preparation: Eat fully ripe (soft, wrinkled). Dry the ripe fruit for winter stores.

codex: A living fossil, planted at temples for a thousand years. The nut is food and a small poison both — the old rule is ten a day, roasted, and never for children.
description: a fan-leafed tree dropping foul-smelling yellow fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Ginkgo. Fan-shaped leaves, foul yellow fruit on the ground.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the inner kernel only. The flesh stinks and burns skin; the kernel must be roasted. Contains ginkgotoxin — dose matters.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: roasted kernels, ~10 a day max for adults. A documented poisoning case came from 50 roasted nuts — seizures. Respect the limit.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: crack, roast 25 minutes until the shell splits. Store dry. The street and temple trees are the reliable producers.

lookalikeNote: The fleshy outer coat stinks of rancid butter and blisters skin — wash the nuts with gloves or sticks, then crack and roast the inner kernel. Never eat the flesh.
name: Ginkgo Nut
preparation: Remove the stinking flesh, wash, roast or boil the kernel ~25 minutes. Limit: about 10 nuts a day for adults; children far fewer. Raw or excess nuts cause vomiting and seizures (ginkgotoxin, 4'-O-methylpyridoxine).

codex: The burrs do the guarding; the fire does the cooking. A chestnut lane in fall is a pantry with thorns.
description: a spreading tree with spiny green burrs splitting open in fall

knowledgeLevels.1: Chestnut. Spiny burrs splitting to show brown nuts.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the nut (score and roast; raw is tannic). Not the glossy horse chestnut — different tree, poisonous.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: roasted or boiled — real starch calories, stores weeks cool and dry. Gather fast; everything else wants them too.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: float-test in water (sinkers keep). Roast cut-side up. 2x yield from the old lane trees.

lookalikeNote: Horse chestnut (Aesculus) is NOT food: its seed is glossy mahogany with a big pale scar and no pointed tip, and it's bitter with saponins. True chestnut has a pointed tip and a small scar — roast it.
name: Chinese Chestnut
preparation: Score the shell, roast or boil. Raw chestnuts are tannic and hard to digest.

codex: The ancestor of every soybean on earth, still twining along the field edges. Protein that asks only for a pot and patience.
description: a twining vine with small hairy pods along field edges

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild soybean. A twining vine with small hairy pods.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the beans (small, dark). Must be cooked — raw beans upset the stomach badly.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: boiled or fermented — dense protein. The ancestor of tofu, miso, and soy sauce.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest when pods rattle. Long-cook with a pinch of ash to soften. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Small black seeds in hairy pods on a twining vine. If the pods are smooth and the vine doesn't twine, it's something else — check before you pick.
name: Wild Soybean
preparation: Boil the beans well — raw soybeans carry trypsin inhibitors that punish the gut. Ferment or long-cook.

codex: Flower above, dinner below. The root keeps its crunch for months in cold mud — the pond is a root cellar that waters itself.
description: broad leaves standing tall above still water on stiff stalks

knowledgeLevels.1: Lotus. Big round leaves standing up out of still water.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the root (white, jointed, crunchy). Dig it from the mud under the standing leaves.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: starch and crunch — slice for soup, fry for chips. The seeds in the pod are food too.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: feel for the joints in the mud before you dig. Harvest in fall when the starch peaks. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Lotus leaves stand ABOVE the water on stiff stalks; water-lily pads float flat. Only the standing-leaf plant hides the crisp white root.
name: Lotus Root
preparation: Dig from the mud, peel, slice. Good raw, better cooked; the segments keep crisp in stir-fry.

uses.note: root fresh, boiled, or fried; seeds too

codex: The silvery underside is the signature — flip the leaf and it flashes white. Moxa, dumplings, and the taste of spring rain.
description: a knee-high herb with silvery-white leaf undersides

knowledgeLevels.1: Mugwort. Knee-high, silvery-white under the leaves.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the young shoots and leaves (pound into dumplings, dry for tea). Medicinal too — the old moxa herb.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: spring greens, stomach-settling tea. Harvest before it flowers for the tenderest tips.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: take the top 10cm only; it re-sprouts. Dry bundles for winter tea. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Flip the leaf: mugwort flashes silvery-white underneath and smells sharp-herbal when crushed. Young chrysanthemum looks similar but lacks the silver back — smell and flip before you pick.
name: Mugwort
preparation: Eat the young shoots fresh or pounded into dumplings; dry for tea. The silver underside is the ID.

codex: The vine is the enemy and the root is the prize — three feet of starch hiding under the tangle. Kuzu: the thickener emperors ate.
description: a vast tangle of vines with huge leaves, roots like buried logs

knowledgeLevels.1: Kudzu. A tangle of vines swallowing the treeline.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the root — enormous, starchy. Dig in winter when the sap is down. The starch must be washed out and settled.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: kuzu starch for thickening, dumplings, noodles. The flowers make jelly; the young shoots are greens.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: follow the oldest vine to the crown root. Pound, wash, settle, dry — the white cake keeps for years. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Kudzu's leaves are big three-lobed affairs on a hairy vine. The prize is the crown root — dig where the oldest stem meets the ground.
name: Kudzu Root
preparation: Dig the root (winter is best), pound and wash the starch out, settle and dry. Cook the starch — dumplings, thickener, noodles.

codex: The old mountain vegetable. Boil it, change the water, and respect the dose — bracken asks for moderation, not abstinence.
description: tightly coiled green fiddleheads unfurling into triangle fronds

knowledgeLevels.1: Bracken. Coiled fiddleheads opening into triangle fronds.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the young fiddleheads only. Boil and discard the water — bracken carries ptaquiloside, a carcinogen. Small amounts, rarely.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: a traditional spring vegetable across East Asia. Boiled, shocked, dressed. Never eat mature fronds.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick under 15cm, tight coils only. Double-boil for safety. A seasonal treat, not a staple.

lookalikeNote: True fiddleheads of bracken unfurl from fuzzy coils into triangular fronds. If the coil has a deep U-shaped groove and brown papery scales, that's ostrich fern — a different, safer fiddlehead.
name: Bracken Fiddlehead
preparation: Boil the young fiddleheads and discard the water (ptaquiloside). Eat sparingly and seasonally — never a daily staple.

codex: The invader that eats hillsides — and the spring vegetable that eats back. Tart as rhubarb, free as weeds.
description: red-speckled hollow shoots with heart-shaped leaves by the water

knowledgeLevels.1: Knotweed. Hollow red-speckled shoots by the water.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young shoots under 30cm, tart like rhubarb. Oxalic acid — don't live on it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: spring vegetable, jam, pie filling. Peel the older shoots.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: snap-clean shoots only. The patch you harvest is the patch you control. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Young knotweed shoots look like red asparagus with heart-shaped leaves. Only the young shoots are food — once the stems toughen and the leaves broaden, it's fiber, not dinner.
name: Knotweed Shoot
preparation: Eat young shoots raw or cooked; tart like rhubarb. Oxalic acid — moderate amounts.

codex: Crisp white corms under the mud — the water chestnut doesn't taste like much until you need crunch more than flavor.
description: spiky grass tufts in the shallows hiding crisp round corms

knowledgeLevels.1: Water chestnut. Spiky grass in the shallows.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the round corms in the mud. Peel, and always cook — ditch water carries flukes.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: crunch that survives cooking — stir-fry, soup, ground for flour.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: rake the mud in fall when the tops brown. Keep peeled corms in clean water. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: True water chestnut is a sedge — spiky grass-like tufts, round crisp corms. Don't confuse with ornamental water plants; if the corm isn't crisp-white inside, don't eat it.
name: Water Chestnut
preparation: Dig the corms, peel, and boil or stir-fry. Always cook — paddy and ditch water can carry parasites.

codex: Flat leaves, garlic breath. The dumpling herb — cut it and it comes back, cut it and it comes back.
description: a clump of flat grass-like leaves smelling of garlic when bruised

knowledgeLevels.1: Garlic chives. Flat leaves, garlic smell when bruised.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves and unopened buds. The smell is the ID — no garlic smell, no chive.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: dumplings, pancakes, stir-fry. Cut-and-come-again all season.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: cut 5cm above the crown and it regrows in weeks. Divide clumps in fall. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: The garlic smell is the whole test: crush a leaf. True garlic chives smell of garlic. Any grass-like leaf that doesn't is not food.
name: Chinese Chive
preparation: Eat fresh or cooked. The unopened flower buds are the best part.

uses.note: leaves and buds, fresh or cooked

codex: The little heart-pods give it away. A weed of every continent that followed humans here and stayed for dinner.
description: a low rosette with tiny heart-shaped seed pods on wiry stems

knowledgeLevels.1: Shepherd's purse. Tiny heart-shaped pods on wiry stems.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young rosette leaves and the peppery seed pods. A classic spring green.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: soup, dumplings, porridge herb. Vitamin C when you need it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: gather rosettes before the stem bolts. The pods dry for a peppery seasoning. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: The heart-shaped (triangular) seed pods are unmistakable — no lookalike carries them. Rosette leaves are best before the stem shoots up.
name: Shepherd's Purse
preparation: Eat young leaves raw or cooked; the seed pods are peppery. A safe beginner green.

codex: Red lanterns on a thorny shrub. The birds strip them by fall's end — pick with them, not after them.
description: a thorny arching shrub hung with small oblong red berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Goji. Small red berries on a thorny shrub.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the ripe berries — soft, sweet-tart. Dry them like raisins.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: trail food, soup, tea. Stores dried for months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shake the branches over a cloth. Dry in the sun until leathery. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Goji grows on a thorny UPRIGHT shrub. Bittersweet nightshade makes similar red berries but on a CLIMBING vine with purple star flowers — that one is poison. Shrub = goji; vine = walk away.
name: Goji Berry
preparation: Eat ripe berries fresh or dried. The thorny shrub is the ID — never pick red berries off a vine.

codex: Apple-crisp fresh, date-sweet dried. The tree fruits whether or not anyone is watching — plant once, eat for a lifetime.
description: a small thorny tree with wrinkled reddish-brown fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Jujube. Small tree, wrinkled red-brown fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the fruit — crisp like apple when fresh, sweet like dates dried.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fresh eating, dried for winter, boiled into tonic soups.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest at full red-brown. Dry on the branch or in the sun. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Ripe jujubes are deep red-brown and wrinkled like big dates. Unripe ones are green-yellow and bland — wait for the wrinkle.
name: Jujube
preparation: Eat fresh when crisp; dry for winter stores. The wrinkled red fruit is ripe.

codex: The silkworm tree, feeding whoever's hungry now. Wait for the dark ones — the white ones are a lesson in patience.
description: a fast-growing tree dropping dark purple berries that stain the ground

knowledgeLevels.1: Mulberry. Dark purple berries staining the ground purple.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe berries only — dark, soft, sweet. Unripe white/green ones with milky sap cause nausea.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fresh eating, jam, dried. The leaves feed silkworms — a trade good if anyone's raising them.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: spread a cloth and shake. The ripe ones fall; the unripe ones cling. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Only the dark, soft, sweet berries are food. White or green berries with milky sap will turn your stomach — patience is the whole technique.
name: White Mulberry
preparation: Eat ripe (dark, soft) berries fresh or dried. Avoid unripe white/green fruit.

uses.note: ripe berries fresh, dried, or jam

codex: Spring fruit on an evergreen tree — the loquat fruits while everything else is still waking up. Sweet flesh, treacherous seeds.
description: an evergreen tree with big veined leaves and clusters of yellow-orange fruit

knowledgeLevels.1: Loquat. Yellow-orange fruit in clusters on an evergreen tree.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the flesh only. The big brown seeds carry amygdalin — spit them out, don't chew them.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: spring fruit when little else is ripe. Jam, poached, fresh.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick fully yellow-soft. The seeds are large — teach everyone to spit. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: The flesh is safe and sweet; the SEEDS are the danger (cyanide compounds if chewed). Eat the fruit, spit the seeds — every time.
name: Loquat
preparation: Eat the ripe flesh fresh or as jam. Always spit out the seeds — they contain amygdalin.

codex: Square stem, serrated leaf, unmistakable smell. The mint family's loud cousin — crush it and there's no doubt.
description: a bushy herb with serrated purple-green leaves on square stems

knowledgeLevels.1: Perilla. Serrated leaves, square stems, strong smell when crushed.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the leaves — the smell is the ID. Wraps, pickles, seasoning.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fresh wraps for anything rich; dried and salted for winter.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pinch the tops to bush it out. It self-seeds — let one plant go and you'll never plant again. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Crush the leaf: true perilla smells sharp and unmistakable, and the stem is square (mint family). No smell + round stem = not perilla.
name: Perilla (Shiso)
preparation: Eat fresh as wraps or pickled. The smell test is the ID.

codex: Tong ho — the chrysanthemum you eat. Floral, green, a little wild; the hot-pot herb that grows itself.
description: a feathery-leaved herb with daisy-like buds, smelling faintly floral

knowledgeLevels.1: Edible chrysanthemum. Feathery leaves, faint floral smell.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves and stems. A classic hot-pot green.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: quick-cooked greens, soup herb. Cut and it regrows.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest before buds open for the tenderest leaves. Succession-sow the patch. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Edible chrysanthemum smells faintly floral-sweet when crushed, and the leaves are deeply cut and feathery. Ornamental mums smell sharp-medicinal — eat only the sweet-smelling one.
name: Chrysanthemum Greens
preparation: Cook the young leaves briefly — hot-pot style. Best before flowering.

codex: The patient root. Peel it like it owes you money, cook it like you mean it, and it feeds you like a potato that went to finishing school.
description: big heart-shaped leaves on stalks rising from a muddy corm

knowledgeLevels.1: Taro. Big heart-shaped leaves, starchy corm in the mud.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the corm (and young leaves, cooked long). Raw taro is full of calcium-oxalate needles — it will set your mouth on fire.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: boiled, steamed, roasted — dense starch. Peel with care; the raw juice itches.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: smaller corms cook faster and itch less. Always cook through — no pink centers, no raw bites. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Edible taro's leaf stalk joins the leaf near its center (peltate). If the stalk joins at the leaf EDGE, that's Alocasia — far more acrid, leave it alone. And never eat any of it raw.
name: Taro
preparation: Peel carefully (raw juice irritates skin), then boil, steam, or roast until fully soft. Never eat raw — calcium oxalate raphides.

codex: The field weed that never left. Peppery greens in spring, sharp seeds in fall — the mustard that feeds twice.
description: a weedy mustard with yellow flowers and peppery basal leaves

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild mustard. Yellow flowers, peppery leaves.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves (peppery greens), unopened buds (like tiny broccoli), seeds (mustard).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: spring greens, potherb, seed mustard. A famine food with dignity.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: graze the rosettes before flowering. Save seed heads for seasoning. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Four-petaled yellow flowers and peppery bite = mustard family, safe. The basal rosette is the eating stage; once it bolts tall and tough, take the buds instead.
name: Field Mustard
preparation: Eat young leaves and buds raw or cooked; grind ripe seeds for mustard.

codex: Golden needles — the dried buds chefs pay for. Fresh ones ask for the pot; a few stomachs ask for caution first.
description: tawny trumpet flowers on arching stems, buds like golden needles

knowledgeLevels.1: Daylily. Tawny trumpet flowers, long buds.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: unopened buds (golden needles) — cook them. Some people react to daylily; try a little first.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: buds in soup and stir-fry; dried buds are the prized golden needles.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick buds the day before they'd open. Dry on racks for the winter store. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: True daylily (Hemerocallis) has fibrous roots, not bulbs — if it grows from a true bulb, it's a true lily and may be toxic. Fibrous roots + tawny trumpets = daylily.
name: Daylily Bud
preparation: Cook the unopened buds; dry for golden needles. Try a small portion first — a few people react.

codex: Fish mint. It smells like a tidepool and tastes like one too — an acquired love, and a free salad.
description: heart-shaped leaves in wet ground smelling faintly of fish when crushed

knowledgeLevels.1: Fish mint. Heart-shaped leaves in the wet ground, fishy smell.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves and tender stems. The fishy smell is the ID — nothing else smells like it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: fresh salad herb, cold dishes, soup garnish. Loves wet feet.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: it spreads by runners — contain it or feed the village with it. Pick the tender tops. 2x yield.

lookalikeNote: Crush it: the fishy smell is unmistakable and no lookalike has it. Heart-shaped leaves + wet ground + fish smell = fish mint.
name: Fish Mint
preparation: Eat fresh in salads and cold dishes. The smell cooks off but the crunch stays.

codex: The queen of poisons wears a mountain-green disguise. Every spring someone mistakes her for dinner. Be the someone who doesn't.
description: tall spikes of helmet-shaped purple-blue flowers; young shoots like asparagus

knowledgeLevels.1: Aconite. Helmet-shaped purple-blue flowers on tall spikes.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON: every part carries aconitine — roots, shoots, leaves, flowers. Cooking does NOT detoxify. A few grams can stop a heart.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. It is medicine only in expert hands after elaborate processing, and never yours. Mark every patch.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: learn it so you never pick it. The young shoots mimic edible mountain greens — that mimicry kills. Teach the village the helmet flower.

lookalikeNote: THE KILLER MISTAKE: young aconite shoots look like edible spring mountain greens. Rule: never gather an unidentified spring shoot. The helmet-shaped flower is the giveaway — by then it's too late for whoever picked the shoot.
name: Aconite (Monkshood)
preparation: DO NOT EAT. All parts contain aconitine; cooking does not detoxify. Symptoms: tingling mouth, vomiting, heart arrhythmia — can kill within hours.
sources: FDA Talk Paper T01-19 — Aconitum carmichaelii

codex: The trumpet flower that lies. Its seedlings pass for potherbs — in Guizhou, one bowl of mistaken seedlings killed a family.
description: rank-smelling weed with white trumpet flowers and spiny seed pods

knowledgeLevels.1: Jimsonweed. White trumpet flowers, spiny pods, rank smell.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON: tropane alkaloids — hallucinations, racing heart, death. The SEEDLINGS look like edible greens; that mistake has killed families.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. Not medicine, not food, not worth a second look. Pull it with gloves if it invades the garden.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: teach the seedlings to everyone — toothed oval leaves, rank smell when crushed. If a 'wild vegetable' smells rank and wrong, it is.

lookalikeNote: The seedlings are the trap: gathered as wild greens in China with fatal results (documented Guizhou family poisoning). Mature plant is obvious — trumpet flowers, spiny pods, foul smell. Learn the seedling, not the flower.
name: Jimsonweed
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Tropane alkaloids cause delirium, rapid heartbeat, and death. Seedlings have been fatally mistaken for edible greens.
sources: BMC Pharmacology and Toxicology — Guizhou Datura case

codex: The parsnip that isn't. White roots, yellow sap, a smell like the vegetable drawer — and enough cicutoxin in one bite to end you.
description: white umbrella flowers over hollow purple-streaked stems in the marsh

knowledgeLevels.1: Water hemlock. White umbrella flowers, hollow stems, marsh ground.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON: the white tuberous roots look like wild parsnip. One bite can kill — cicutoxin, seizures, no antidote.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. Cut the stem and yellow oily sap oozes out, smelling of parsnip — that's the warning.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the stem base is swollen, the leaf veins end in the notches (not the tips) — unique in the family. Teach it; the marsh is full of it.

lookalikeNote: Mistaken for wild parsnip: white clustered roots, parsnip smell. Tell it by the swollen stem base and the yellow oily sap from a cut stem. Water parsnip lacks both. When in doubt in the marsh, eat nothing root-shaped.
name: Water Hemlock
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Cicutoxin causes seizures and respiratory paralysis; a 2-3cm piece of root can be fatal. No antidote.
sources: CDC MMWR — Water Hemlock Poisoning, Maine 1992

codex: The vine that apes the goji. Red berries, purple stars — pretty, climbing, and full of solanine.
description: a scrambling vine with purple star flowers maturing to red oval berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Bittersweet nightshade. Purple star flowers, red berries, climbing vine.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON: solanine in the berries — nausea, vomiting, worse in quantity. The berries ape goji at a glance.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. The vine climbs; the shrub stands — that's the whole distinction.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: drill the village: goji grows on a thorny UPRIGHT shrub; nightshade CLIMBS with purple flowers. Never pick red berries off a vine.

lookalikeNote: Goji's red berries grow on a thorny upright SHRUB. Nightshade's grow on a CLIMBING vine with purple star-shaped flowers. Shrub = goji; vine = poison. This is the pair that tests whether you learned the goji lesson.
name: Bittersweet Nightshade
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Berries contain solanine — gastrointestinal poisoning. Easily confused with goji at a glance; check the growth habit.
